meta.subject: maths
meta.title: Trigonometry: ratios, identities and heights & distances
meta.source_edition: NCERT Reprint 2026-27, Class 10 Mathematics, Ch 8 (jemh108.pdf, printed pages 113-132) and Ch 9 Some Applications of Trigonometry (jemh109.pdf, printed pages 133-143)

board_asks: finding all six ratios from one, evaluating expressions at the specific angles (0/30/45/60/90), proving trigonometric identities, and one heights-and-distances word problem (angle of elevation / depression — only 30°, 45°, 60°, at most two right triangles). The identity manipulations, the specific-angle table and the heights-and-distances figure carry almost every mark here.

big_idea.body: Fix an acute angle in a right triangle and the ratios of its sides stop depending on how big the triangle is - they depend only on the angle. Those six fixed numbers are the trigonometric ratios (sin, cos, tan and their reciprocals cosec, sec, cot). This chapter does three things: defines the ratios, pins down their exact values at $0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°$, and proves the identity $\sin^2 A + \cos^2 A = 1$ (with its two cousins) that turns messy expressions into $1$. The applications chapter (Ch 9) then turns a real scene - a tower, a kite, a ship seen from a lighthouse - into a right triangle whose angle of elevation or depression you know, so one trigonometric ratio gives the height or distance you cannot measure.

definitions.verbatim: Trigonometry is the study of relationships between the sides and angles of a triangle.
definitions.plain: the word comes from the Greek $tri$ (three), $gon$ (sides), $metron$ (measure). In Class 10 we study it for the acute angles of a right triangle only.

definitions.verbatim: We call it the side opposite to angle A. AC is the hypotenuse of the right triangle and the side AB is a part of ∠A. So, we call it the side adjacent to angle A.
definitions.plain: name the three sides relative to the angle you are working with: the side facing the angle is opposite, the longest side (facing the right angle) is the hypotenuse, the third is adjacent. Switch to angle C and opposite/adjacent swap.

definitions.verbatim: So, the trigonometric ratios of an acute angle in a right triangle express the relationship between the angle and the length of its sides.
definitions.plain: $\sin A = \dfrac{\text{opp}}{\text{hyp}}$, $\cos A = \dfrac{\text{adj}}{\text{hyp}}$, $\tan A = \dfrac{\text{opp}}{\text{adj}}$. Memorise them against the labelled triangle, not as isolated letters.

definitions.verbatim: The values of the trigonometric ratios of an angle do not vary with the lengths of the sides of the triangle, if the angle remains the same.
definitions.plain: this is why the ratios are well defined - proved by AA similarity. It lets you set the sides as $k, 2k, \dots$ (any positive $k$): the ratio cancels $k$, so the answer never depends on your choice.

definitions.verbatim: An equation involving trigonometric ratios of an angle is called a trigonometric identity, if it is true for all values of the angle(s) involved.
definitions.plain: an identity holds for every valid angle, so you prove it by algebra, not by plugging in one value. To prove one, transform the LHS until it becomes the RHS.

definitions.verbatim: The ratios defined above are abbreviated as sin A, cos A, tan A, cosec A, sec A and cot A respectively. Note that the ratios cosec A, sec A and cot A are respectively, the reciprocals of the ratios sin A, cos A and tan A.

definitions.term: sin A, cos A never exceed 1
definitions.verbatim: Since the hypotenuse is the longest side in a right triangle, the value of sin A or cos A is always less than 1 (or, in particular, equal to 1).

source.note: NCERT's printed phrasing 'less than 1 (or, in particular, equal to 1)' means sin A, cos A are at most 1; preserved verbatim

definitions.term: sin A is not sin times A
definitions.verbatim: sin A is not the product of ‘sin’ and A. ‘sin’ separated from A has no meaning.

The angle of elevation of an object viewed, is the angle formed by the line of sight with the horizontal when it is above the horizontal level, i.e., the case when we raise our head to look at the object.
definitions.plain: you look up at the object: the angle between the horizontal through your eye and the line of sight. It sits at the observer, never at the top of the tower.

source.note: Ch 9 Some Applications of Trigonometry, Summary point 1(ii); introduced in the body on p.133-134

definitions.verbatim: The angle of depression of an object viewed, is the angle formed by the line of sight with the horizontal when it is below the horizontal level, i.e., the case when we lower our head to look at the object.
definitions.plain: you look down at the object: the angle between the horizontal through your eye and the line of sight. By alternate angles it equals the angle of elevation of your eye from that object - which is how it enters the right triangle on the ground.

source.note: Ch 9 Summary point 1(iii); introduced in the body on p.134

definitions.verbatim: Thus, the line of sight is the line drawn from the eye of an observer to the point in the object viewed by the observer.

concepts.title: Find every ratio from one
concepts.body: Given one ratio, draw a right triangle and mark the two sides in that ratio as multiples of $k$ (e.g. $\tan A = \tfrac43 \Rightarrow$ opposite $=4k$, adjacent $=3k$). Get the third side by Pythagoras, then read all six ratios straight off - $k$ always cancels.

concepts.title: Ratios of the specific angles
concepts.body: The exact values at $0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°$ come from the $45$-$45$-$90$ and $30$-$60$-$90$ triangles (Table 8.1). $\sin$ rises $0 \to 1$, $\cos$ falls $1 \to 0$; $\tan 90°$, $\cot 0°$, $\sec 90°$, $\csc 0°$ are not defined. Learn the table cold - it is assumed in every evaluation question.

concepts.title: The three Pythagorean identities
concepts.body: $\sin^2 A + \cos^2 A = 1$; $\;1 + \tan^2 A = \sec^2 A$ (for $0° \le A < 90°$); $\;1 + \cot^2 A = \csc^2 A$ (for $0° < A \le 90°$). All three come from Pythagoras. Mind the angle ranges - $\tan/\sec$ break at $90°$, $\cot/\csc$ break at $0°$.
concepts.tested: MCQ simplifications like $9\sec^2 A - 9\tan^2 A$ (Exercise 8.3 Q3)

concepts.title: Proving identities (LHS → RHS)
concepts.body: Convert everything to $\sin$ and $\cos$, take a common denominator, and use $\sin^2 A + \cos^2 A = 1$ (often via $1 - \sin^2 A = \cos^2 A$). Work on one side only until it becomes the other - never manipulate both sides at once.

concepts.title: Heights and distances - angle of elevation / depression
concepts.body: Turn the scene into a right triangle: the vertical height, the horizontal distance and the line of sight. Mark the angle of elevation at the observer's eye when the object is above the horizontal, the angle of depression when it is below (alternate angles carry it down to the far end of the triangle). Then pick the one ratio that links the known side and the wanted side - usually $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\text{height}}{\text{distance}}$, or $\sin\theta$ when the hypotenuse (a ladder, a string, a rope) is involved - and read its value from Table 8.1. Board problems use only $30°$, $45°$ and $60°$, and at most two right triangles (a flagstaff on a building, two ships from a lighthouse, a shadow at two altitudes); add the observer's height at the end if the eye is above the ground.
concepts.tested: 2-mark one-triangle problem (Exercise 9.1 Q1, Q4) · 3-mark two-triangle problem (Exercise 9.1 Q7, Q13)

source.note: method on p.135 (choose tan A or cot A); the 30°/45°/60° and two-right-triangle limits are the CBSE 2026-27 syllabus's own restriction (Maths p.6)

examples.shape: All ratios from one · NCERT Example 1
examples.problem_verbatim: Given tan A = 4/3, find the other trigonometric ratios of the angle A.

solution_steps.text: $\tan A = \dfrac{BC}{AB} = \dfrac{4}{3}$, so take $BC = 4k$ and $AB = 3k$ for a positive number $k$.
solution_steps.concept_tag: assign sides in the given ratio

examples.mark_logic: 3-mark shape: correct side ratio + Pythagoras (1) · $\sin A$ and $\cos A$ (1) · the three reciprocal ratios (1). Setting the sides as $4k, 3k$ keeps the answer independent of $k$ - the whole point of the ratios.

examples.problem_verbatim: Consider △ACB, right-angled at C, in which AB = 29 units, BC = 21 units and ∠ABC = θ (see Fig. 8.10). Determine the values of (i) cos²θ + sin²θ, (ii) cos²θ – sin²θ

solution_steps.lead: Write the two ratios for the angle.

examples.mark_logic: 3-mark shape: finding $AC = 20$ by Pythagoras (1) · the two ratios plus part (i) $=1$ (1) · part (ii) $=\tfrac{41}{841}$ (1). Part (i) is exactly $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$ - recognise it and it is a free mark.

examples.problem_verbatim: In △ABC, right-angled at B, AB = 5 cm and ∠ACB = 30° (see Fig. 8.19). Determine the lengths of the sides BC and AC.

solution_steps.lead: Pick the ratio linking the known and unknown.
solution_steps.text: $BC$ is adjacent to $\angle C$ and $AB$ is opposite to it, so $\dfrac{AB}{BC} = \tan C$.

examples.mark_logic: 3-mark shape: correct ratio for $BC$ (1) · $BC = 5\sqrt3$ from $\tan 30°$ (1) · $AC = 10$ from $\sin 30°$ (1). Table 8.1 values must be recalled exactly - a wrong $\tan 30°$ loses the later marks too.

examples.problem_verbatim: Prove that sec A (1 – sin A)(sec A + tan A) = 1.

solution_steps.lead: Convert everything to sin and cos.
solution_steps.text: $\text{LHS} = \sec A\,(1 - \sin A)(\sec A + \tan A) = \dfrac{1}{\cos A}(1 - \sin A)\left(\dfrac{1}{\cos A} + \dfrac{\sin A}{\cos A}\right)$.

solution_steps.lead: Combine into a difference of squares.

solution_steps.text: Since $1 - \sin^2 A = \cos^2 A$, this is $\dfrac{\cos^2 A}{\cos^2 A} = 1 = \text{RHS}$.

examples.mark_logic: 3-mark shape: sec/tan rewritten in $\sin,\cos$ (1) · the $(1-\sin A)(1+\sin A) = 1-\sin^2 A$ step (1) · using $1-\sin^2 A = \cos^2 A$ to reach $1$ (1). Transform the LHS only - never operate on both sides at once.

examples.shape: Height of a tower (one right triangle) · NCERT Ch 9 Example 1
examples.problem_verbatim: A tower stands vertically on the ground. From a point on the ground, which is 15 m away from the foot of the tower, the angle of elevation of the top of the tower is found to be 60°. Find the height of the tower.

solution_steps.lead: Draw the right triangle and choose the ratio.
solution_steps.text: Let $AB$ be the tower and $C$ the point on the ground, so $BC = 15$ m, $\angle ACB = 60°$ and the triangle is right-angled at $B$. The known side $BC$ is adjacent and the wanted side $AB$ is opposite, so use $\tan 60°$.
solution_steps.concept_tag: angle of elevation → tan links height and distance

solution_steps.text: $\tan 60° = \dfrac{AB}{BC} \Rightarrow \sqrt3 = \dfrac{AB}{15} \Rightarrow AB = 15\sqrt3$ m. The height of the tower is $15\sqrt3$ m.
solution_steps.concept_tag: tan 60° = √3 from Table 8.1; answer with unit

examples.mark_logic: 2-mark shape (Section B): 1 for the labelled right triangle with the angle of elevation at the ground point and the correct ratio ($\tan 60°$), 1 for substituting $\sqrt3$ and stating $15\sqrt3$ m with the unit.

examples.shape: Width of a river from angles of depression (two right triangles) · NCERT Ch 9 Example 7
examples.problem_verbatim: From a point on a bridge across a river, the angles of depression of the banks on opposite sides of the river are 30° and 45°, respectively. If the bridge is at a height of 3 m from the banks, find the width of the river.

solution_steps.lead: Set up the two right triangles.
solution_steps.text: Let $A$ and $B$ be the points on the two banks, $P$ the point on the bridge and $D$ the foot of the perpendicular from $P$, so $PD = 3$ m and the width is $AB = AD + DB$. The angles of depression $30°$ and $45°$ become, by alternate angles, $\angle A = 30°$ in right $\triangle APD$ and $\angle B = 45°$ in right $\triangle PBD$.
solution_steps.concept_tag: angle of depression → alternate angle at the bank

solution_steps.text: $\tan 45° = \dfrac{PD}{BD} = 1 \Rightarrow BD = PD = 3$ m. So $AB = BD + AD = 3 + 3\sqrt3 = 3(1 + \sqrt3)$ m - the width of the river.

examples.mark_logic: 3-mark shape (Section C): 1 for the figure with both angles of depression transferred to the banks, 1 for $AD = 3\sqrt3$ m from $\tan 30°$, 1 for $BD = 3$ m from $\tan 45°$ and the width $3(1+\sqrt3)$ m with unit. Marking the angle of depression at the bank instead of at $P$ (with the horizontal) is the classic lost mark.

source.note: problem on p.140, solution runs to p.141

strategies.cue: Given one ratio, want the others?
strategies.text: Draw the triangle, set the two sides as $k$-multiples, get the third by Pythagoras, read off all six.
Substitute straight from Table 8.1. Do not re-derive - recall $\sin, \cos, \tan$ at $0/30/45/60/90$ instantly.
Turn everything into $\sin$ and $\cos$, take a common denominator, apply $\sin^2 A + \cos^2 A = 1$. Work one side only.

strategies.cue: A ratio looks like it could be $>1$?
strategies.text: Check: $\sin A$ and $\cos A$ are at most $1$; $\sec A$ and $\csc A$ are at least $1$. If not, re-check opposite vs adjacent.

strategies.cue: Angle changes from A to C?
strategies.text: Opposite and adjacent swap. Re-label before writing the ratio - this is the most common slip.

Draw the right triangle first, mark the right angle and the angle of elevation / depression at the eye, then write the ONE ratio linking the known and wanted sides (usually $\tan$). Only $30°$, $45°$, $60°$ appear - recall them from Table 8.1.

pitfalls.text: Swapping opposite and adjacent when the angle changes (angle A vs angle C) - re-label the sides against the new angle first.
Claiming $\sin A > 1$ or $\cos A > 1$ - impossible, since the hypotenuse is the longest side.
Reading $\sin A$ as $\sin \times A$ - ‘sin’ with no angle is meaningless.
Writing $0$ or $\infty$ for undefined ratios - $\tan 90°$, $\cot 0°$, $\sec 90°$, $\csc 0°$ are ‘not defined’.
Ignoring the identity's angle range - $1 + \cot^2 A = \csc^2 A$ holds for $0° < A \le 90°$, not at $A = 0°$.
Marking the angle of depression at the foot of the object - it is measured at the observer's eye, below the horizontal; it reaches the ground triangle only as the equal alternate angle.

formula_strip.label: Reciprocals
formula_strip.math: $\csc A = \dfrac{1}{\sin A},\ \sec A = \dfrac{1}{\cos A},\ \cot A = \dfrac{1}{\tan A} = \dfrac{\cos A}{\sin A}$

formula_strip.label: Identities
formula_strip.math: $\sin^2 A + \cos^2 A = 1;\ \ 1 + \tan^2 A = \sec^2 A;\ \ 1 + \cot^2 A = \csc^2 A$

formula_strip.label: Heights & distances
formula_strip.math: $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\text{height}}{\text{horizontal distance}}$ · elevation: look up · depression: look down (= elevation from the other end)

third_tab_content.name: The Pythagorean trigonometric identities
third_tab_content.intro: NCERT proves one identity, $\sin^2 A + \cos^2 A = 1$, directly from the Pythagoras theorem, then derives the other two by dividing the same relation differently. Every identity in the chapter ultimately rests on these three (p.128-129).

steps.claim: Start from Pythagoras in △ABC, right-angled at B.

steps.justification: True for all A with $0° \le A \le 90°$, so it is a trigonometric identity.
$\tan A, \sec A$ are undefined at $90°$, so this holds for $0° \le A < 90°$.
$\cot A, \csc A$ are undefined at $0°$, so this holds for $0° < A \le 90°$.

source.note: identity derivation runs p.128-129 (section 8.4); the three results are collected in Summary point 6, p.132

fig_ratio_triangle_84.caption: Right triangle ABC (right-angled at B): AC is the hypotenuse, BC the side opposite to angle A, AB the side adjacent to angle A - the labels the six ratios are built on.
fig_ratio_triangle_84.legend: Relative to angle A at the bottom-left: the side across from it (BC) is 'opposite', the longest side (AC, across from the right angle) is the 'hypotenuse', the remaining side (AB) is 'adjacent'.
